intro: A fixed probability threshold can be inappropriate when error costs differ. Compare the expected loss of each action and make the tie policy explicit.
task: Choose actions by expected error cost and investigate how asymmetric costs move the probability decision boundary.
requirements: probabilities is a finite vector in [0,1], possibly empty. Both error costs are nonnegative real scalars and their sum must be positive.
Predict one when false_positive_cost*(1-p) <= false_negative_cost*p, including ties. Return dict predictions as integer vector and expected_cost as minimum per-row cost.
Correct decisions have zero cost. Costs are supplied deployment assumptions, and probabilities are assumed to be meaningful conditional estimates.

Numeric inputs must be real and finite with magnitude at most 1e30, except where a stricter bound is stated. Booleans are not numeric parameters. Leave all caller inputs unchanged and raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

hints.title: Write both action costs
hints.body: Predicting positive risks a false positive; predicting negative risks a false negative.

hints.title: A threshold is derived, not fixed
hints.body: For positive total cost the boundary is fp_cost/(fp_cost+fn_cost).

explanation: Expected loss turns a probability estimate into a decision using an explicit utility model. Unequal error costs shift the decision boundary away from one half.
A cost-optimal rule can still perform badly when probabilities are miscalibrated or costs are wrong. Keeping the per-row expected costs visible helps audit those assumptions.
